ml_models.name: Logistic Regression
ml_models.description: A linear model: one weighted sum of the (standardized) features per class, turned into probabilities via softmax. ml_models.name: Naive Bayes

ml_models.name: SVM (RBF)
ml_models.description: A Support Vector Machine with an RBF (Gaussian) kernel: finds the decision boundary that maximizes the margin between classes, implicitly projecting the standardized features into a higher-dimensional space where a non-linear boundary becomes linear. Unlike every other model here, training cost scales roughly quadratically with the number of rows, which is why this is the slowest model in the entire lineup to train despite being 'classic' ML. A full 231,646-row fit was attempted first and killed after 20+ minutes with no end in sight (RBF-kernel SVC training scales roughly O(n^2), and memory usage was still climbing) — this result trains on a stratified 40,000-row subsample instead, same practical tradeoff made elsewhere in this project for oversized data.

dl_models.name: 1D-CNN
dl_models.description: Treats the 33 standardized packet/session features as a 1-dimensional signal and slides learned convolutional filters across neighboring features, looking for local patterns (e.g. a TCP-flag feature next to a length feature behaving a particular way together) before pooling into a fixed-size representation. Common in the MQTT/network-traffic classification literature this project's survey cites. (See the 'DL Home Turf' tab for a follow-up experiment giving this architecture a genuine packet sequence to convolve over, instead of one packet's unrelated header fields.)

dl_models.name: GRU (Recurrent)
dl_models.description: A Gated Recurrent Unit — the more efficient sibling of the LSTM, both explicitly named in this project's survey as common IDS architectures. Reads the 33 features one at a time as if they were a short time series, carrying a hidden state forward, then classifies from the final hidden state. The features have no real temporal order here, so this tests whether recurrent processing helps or just adds overhead on data that isn't actually sequential. (See the 'DL Home Turf' tab for a follow-up experiment giving this architecture a genuine packet sequence to read, instead of one packet's unrelated header fields relabeled as fake timesteps.)

dl_models.name: RNN (Vanilla)
dl_models.description: A plain (Elman) recurrent network — the architecture GRU and LSTM were both built to fix. Reads the 33 features one at a time, carrying a single hidden state forward with a simple tanh update and no gating mechanism at all. Included as the 'how much do the gates actually buy you' reference point against GRU and LSTM below — vanilla RNNs are known to struggle with longer sequences due to vanishing gradients, which the gated variants were designed to fix.

dl_models.name: LSTM
dl_models.description: Long Short-Term Memory — the original gated recurrent architecture, and (along with GRU) explicitly named in this project's survey as a common IDS approach. Maintains a separate cell state alongside the hidden state, controlled by input/forget/output gates, which is more expressive (and has more parameters) than GRU's single gating mechanism. Same caveat as GRU/RNN: the 33 features have no genuine temporal order here, so this tests whether that extra gating complexity earns its keep on data that isn't actually sequential.

anomaly_models.name: Autoencoder (Anomaly Detector)
anomaly_models.description: An encoder-decoder network trained ONLY on legitimate MQTT traffic to reconstruct its own input. It never sees a single labeled attack example. At test time, any packet the network reconstructs poorly (high error) is flagged as anomalous. This is the semi-supervised approach this project's survey argues FL-IDS research should move toward, since it doesn't need balanced labeled examples of every attack type — useful for catching attack types the model has genuinely never seen labeled, i.e. zero-day detection.

hyperparams.threshold_rule: 95th percentile of reconstruction error on legitimate training data

sequence_models.name: 1D-CNN (Temporal)
sequence_models.description: The same 1D-CNN idea as the flat-feature version, but now convolving across real TIME: input is 8 consecutive packets from the same TCP/MQTT session (tcp.stream), with the 33 engineered features as channels. This is the architecture's actual home turf -- local patterns across a short packet run, not across unrelated header fields.

hyperparams.split: stream-level (whole flows held out, zero packet overlap)

This is the architecture's actual home turf -- local patterns across a short packet run, not across unrelated header fields.

hyperparams.split: stream-level (whole flows held out, zero packet overlap)

flat.name: GRU (Recurrent)
flat.description: A Gated Recurrent Unit — the more efficient sibling of the LSTM, both explicitly named in this project's survey as common IDS architectures. Reads the 33 features one at a time as if they were a short time series, carrying a hidden state forward, then classifies from the final hidden state. The features have no real temporal order here, so this tests whether recurrent processing helps or just adds overhead on data that isn't actually sequential. (See the 'DL Home Turf' tab for a follow-up experiment giving this architecture a genuine packet sequence to read, instead of one packet's unrelated header fields relabeled as fake timesteps.)

temporal.name: GRU (Temporal)
temporal.description: The same GRU idea as the flat-feature version, but now reading 8 consecutive real packets from the same session one at a time (33 features per step), instead of 33 unrelated header fields relabeled as fake timesteps. This is what a recurrent network is actually designed to do: carry state across a genuine sequence of events.

hyperparams.split: stream-level (whole flows held out, zero packet overlap)
